group: PSI Score: Pneumonia Severity Index for CAP
question:
Patient note:
A 67-year-old man who retired from his job as a municipal building inspector two years ago arrived in the emergency department just after noon because of forty-eight hours of feverishness, progressively productive cough, and new dull discomfort when he takes a deep breath along the right posterior chest; he reports the sputum changed from clear to yellow this morning and that walking up the eight steps from his driveway left him mildly winded for the first time. In order “to give the doctors a clean slate,” he skipped the morning doses of his usual medications—tenofovir disoproxil fumarate for chronic hepatitis B, a nightly proton-pump inhibitor, and an as-needed proton pump inhibitor—and avoided acetaminophen, cough syrup, or any inhalers despite owning a rescue albuterol canister last used during a viral illness months ago. He drove himself the twenty minutes from his suburban home, breathing only room air during the trip, and drank only water en route. Past medical background is notable for long-standing viral hepatitis that was diagnosed fifteen years earlier and has been characterized by compensated hepatic fibrosis without prior episodes of ascites, encephalopathy, or esophageal variceal bleeding; the most recent outpatient laboratory panel six weeks ago showed a normal total bilirubin, mildly elevated alanine aminotransferase, and an international normalized ratio of 1.1. He has never been told he has kidney trouble, and baseline creatinine values have remained below 1.1 mg/dL; he likewise denies ever experiencing transient neurologic deficits or weakness suggestive of cerebrovascular events and states that, apart from occasional tension headaches, he has never needed to consult a neurologist. He has no known structural or ischemic heart disease, has never been prescribed a diuretic or beta-blocker, and walked three miles every other morning until this week’s illness curtailed his routine. Immunizations are up to date according to the state registry, including both pneumococcal series and the current influenza season. He quit a fifteen-pack-year cigarette habit two decades ago, drinks a single glass of wine only on New Year’s Eve since his hepatologist advised stricter abstinence, and denies any illicit drug use. Family history is unremarkable for premature coronary artery disease or cerebrovascular events. On arrival he was seated upright on the stretcher, answering questions in unhurried complete sentences, accurately reciting the date, location, and current political administration, and recalling three objects at five minutes. His skin felt warm with a light sheen of perspiration; mucous membranes were moist, sclerae anicteric, and there were no spider angiomata or palmar erythema. Untreated triage vitals measured on ambient air at this sea-level facility were: oral temperature 38.2 °C, regular tachycardic radial pulse 104 beats per minute verified by a three-lead monitor as sinus rhythm without ectopy, non-invasive blood pressure 121/72 mm Hg corroborated manually, respirations counted quietly for a full minute at 23 breaths per minute with mild intercostal effort but no supraclavicular retractions, and fingertip pulse oximetry fluctuating between 92 % and 93 %. Neck veins were flat at 45°, and no peripheral edema was noted. Cardiac examination revealed crisp S1 and S2 without murmurs, rubs, or gallops. Pulmonary auscultation demonstrated scattered coarse crackles and bronchial breath sounds over the right mid-posterior lung field with preserved resonance to percussion; the left lung transmitted vesicular airflow throughout, and diaphragmatic excursion was symmetric. The abdomen was soft; the liver edge was palpable 1 cm below the costal margin, smooth and mildly tender to deep palpation, and there was no shifting dullness. A focused neurologic screen showed equal, briskly reactive pupils, intact extra-ocular movements, 5/5 strength in all extremities, and normal rapid alternating movements. Point-of-care capillary glucose obtained prior to venipuncture read 118 mg/dL. Peripheral venous blood and a right radial arterial sample were drawn within ten minutes of bay entry before any intravenous fluids, antimicrobials, or saline flushes larger than the 3 mL used to lock the catheter. The basic metabolic panel returned sodium 141 mEq/L, potassium 4.0 mEq/L, chloride 103 mEq/L, bicarbonate 24 mEq/L, blood urea nitrogen 24 mg/dL, and creatinine 1.0 mg/dL. Complete blood count demonstrated leukocytosis to 12.9 × 10⁹/L with 85 % segmented neutrophils, hematocrit 39 %, hemoglobin 13.2 g/dL, and platelets 172 × 10⁹/L. The arterial blood gas, while he continued to breathe room air, revealed pH 7.40, PaCO₂ 36 mm Hg, PaO₂ 74 mm Hg, and calculated bicarbonate 22 mEq/L, indicating mild hypoxemia without a significant acid–base disturbance. Serum lactate was 1.7 mmol/L, and high-sensitivity troponin I fell below the analytic threshold. A portable postero-anterior chest radiograph obtained fifteen minutes after arrival—prior to any therapy—showed a patchy consolidation in the right lower lobe with air bronchograms, clear costophrenic angles, a normal cardiac silhouette, and no layering opacity to suggest fluid collection. Electrocardiography displayed sinus tachycardia at 103 bpm with normal intervals and nonspecific T-wave flattening but no acute ischemic changes. Two sets of peripheral blood cultures, a voluntary expectorated sputum specimen, urinary antigens for Streptococcus pneumoniae and Legionella pneumophila, and a multiplex respiratory viral PCR panel were dispatched to the laboratory before the first empirical antibiotic dose. Up to the moment this narrative is dictated, he has received no intravenous crystalloids, antipyretics, bronchodilators, corticosteroids, or supplemental oxygen, ensuring that every physiologic observation, laboratory datum, and imaging finding listed above reflects his untreated presentation.

Question: What is the patient's Pneumonia Severity Index (PSI)? You should use the patient's medical values and health status when they were first admitted to the hospital prior to any treatment.
solution:
The Pneumonia Severity Index (PSI) adds demographic, comorbidity, examination, laboratory, and imaging points using untreated admission findings.
- Demographics: A 67-year-old man receives 67 age points. He lives at home, so nursing-home residence adds 0.
- Comorbidities: Chronic hepatitis B with hepatic fibrosis qualifies as liver disease (+20). No malignancy, heart failure, cerebrovascular disease, or renal disease is documented (0 each).
- Examination: He is oriented (0); respiratory rate 23 is <30/min (0); systolic BP 121 is ≥90 mm Hg (0); temperature 38.2 °C is neither <35 nor ≥40 °C (0); pulse 104 is <125/min (0).
- Laboratory findings: pH 7.40 is ≥7.35 (0), BUN 24 is <30 mg/dL (0), sodium 141 is ≥130 mEq/L (0), glucose 118 is <250 mg/dL (0), and hematocrit 39% is ≥30% (0). Room-air PaO₂ 74 mm Hg and saturation 92–93% are above the hypoxemia cutoffs of <60 mm Hg or <90% (0).
- Imaging: Consolidation without pleural effusion adds 0.
Total = 67 + 20 + 0 = 87 (PSI class III).
Final answer: 87
